sp.speaker: PYTHAGORAS
sp.p: Madam, I plainly receive that the perfection of your brightness hath pierced through the thickness that covered my mind, insomuch that I am no less glad to be reformed than ashamed to remember my grossness.

sp.speaker: GYPTES
sp.p: They are thrice fortunate that live in your palace, where truth is not in colours but life, virtues not in imagination but execution.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: I have always studied to have rather living virtues than painted gods, the body of truth than the tomb. But let us walk to Endymion; it may be it lieth in your arts to deliver him. As for Eumenides, I fear he is dead.

sp.speaker: PYTHAGORAS
sp.p: I have alleged all the natural reasons I can for such a long sleep.

sp.speaker: GYPTES
sp.p: I can do nothing till I see him.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Come, Floscula, I am sure you are glad that you shall behold Endymion.

sp.speaker: FLOSCULA
sp.p: I were blessed if I might have him recovered.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Are you in love with his person?

sp.speaker: FLOSCULA
sp.p: No, but with his virtue.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: What say you, Semele?

sp.speaker: SEMELE
sp.p: Madam, I dare say nothing for fear I offend.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Belike you cannot speak except you be spiteful. But as good be silent as saucy. Panelion, what punishment were fit for Semele, in whose speech and thoughts is only contempt and sourness?

sp.speaker: PANELION
sp.p: I love not, madam, to give any judgement. Yet sith Your Highness commandeth: I think, to commit her tongue close prisoner to her mouth.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Agreed. Semele, if thou speak this twelvemonth, thou shalt forfeit thy tongue. –Behold Endymion. Alas, poor gentleman, hast thou spent thy youth in sleep, that once vowed all to my service? Hollow eyes? Grey hairs? Wrinkled cheeks? And decayed limbs? Is it destiny or deceit that hath brought this to pass? If the first, who could prevent thy wretched stars? If the latter, I would I might know thy cruel enemy. I favoured thee, Endymion, for thy honour, thy virtues, thy affections; but to bring thy thoughts within the compass of thy fortunes, I have seemed strange, that I might have thee stayed. And now are thy days ended before my favour begin. But whom have we here? Is it not Corsites?

sp.speaker: ZONTES
sp.p: It is, but more like a leopard than a man.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Awake him. [Corsites is awakened.] How now, Corsites, what make you here? How came you deformed? Look on thy hands, and then thou seest the picture of thy face.

sp.speaker: CORSITES
sp.p: Miserable wretch, and accursed! How am I deluded? Madam, I ask pardon for my offence, and you see my fortune deserveth pity.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Speak on. Thy offence cannot deserve greater punishment; but see thou rehearse the truth, else shalt thou not find me as thou wishest me.

sp.speaker: CORSITES
sp.p: Madam, as it is no offence to be in love, being a man mortal, so I hope can it be no shame to tell with whom, my lady being heavenly. Your Majesty committed to my charge fair Tellus, whose beauty in the same moment took my heart captive that I undertook to carry her body prisoner. Since that time have I found such combats in my thoughts between love and duty, reverence and affection, that I could neither endure the conflict nor hope for the conquest.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: In love? A thing far unfitting the name of a captain, and, as I thought, the tough and unsmoothed nature of Corsites. But forth.

sp.speaker: CORSITES
sp.p: Feeling this continual war, I thought rather by parley to yield than by certain danger to perish. I unfolded to Tellus the depth of my affections, and framed my tongue to utter a sweet tale of love, that was wont to sound nothing but threats of love. She, too fair to be true and too false for one so fair, after a nice denial practised a notable deceit, commanding me to remove Endymion from this cabin and carry him to some dark cave, which I, seeking to accomplish, found impossible, and so by fairies or fiends have been thus handled.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: How say you, my lords, is not Tellus always practising of some deceits? –In sooth, Corsites, thy face is now too foul for a lover and thine heart too fond for a soldier. You may see, when warriors become wantons, how their manners alter with their faces. Is it not a shame, Corsites, that, having lived so long in Mars his camp, thou shouldst now be rocked in Venus' cradle? Dost thou wear Cupid's quiver at thy girdle, and make lances of looks? Well, Corsites, rouse thyself and be as thou hast been, and let Tellus, who is made all of love, melt herself in her own looseness.

sp.speaker: CORSITES
sp.p: Madam, I doubt not but to recover my former state, for Tellus' beauty never wrought such love in my mind as now her deceit hath despite; and yet to be revenged of a woman were a thing than love itself more womanish.

sp.speaker: GYPTES
sp.p: These spots, gentleman, are to be worn out if you rub them over with this lunary, so that in place where you received this maim you shall find a medicine.

sp.speaker: CORSITES
sp.p: I thank you for that. The gods bless me from love and these pretty ladies that haunt this green!

sp.speaker: FLOSCULA
sp.p: Corsites, I would Tellus saw your amiable face.

div2.stage: [Corsites rubs out his spots with lunary from the bank.

sp.speaker: ZONTES
sp.p: How spitefully Semele laugheth, that dare not speak!

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Could you not stir Endymion with that doubled strength of yours?

sp.speaker: CORSITES
sp.p: Not so much as his finger with all my force.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Pythagoras and Gyptes, what think you of Endymion? What reason is to be given, what remedy?

sp.speaker: PYTHAGORAS
sp.p: Madam, it is impossible to yield reason for things that happen not in compass of nature. It is most certain that some strange enchantment hath bound all his senses.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: What say you, Gyptes?

sp.speaker: GYPTES
sp.p: With Pythagoras, that it is enchantment, and that so strange that no art can undo it, for that heaviness argueth a malice unremovable in the enchantress, and that no power can end it till she die that did it or the heavens show some means more than miraculous.

sp.speaker: FLOSCULA
sp.p: O Endymion, could spite itself a mischief so monstrous as to make thee dead with life, and living being altogether dead? Where others number their years, their hours, their minutes, and step to age by stairs, thou only hast thy years and times in a cluster, being old before thou rememberest thou wast young.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: No more, Floscula; pity doth him no good. I would anything else might, and I vow by the unspotted honour of a lady he should not miss it. But is this all, Gyptes, that is to be done?

sp.speaker: GYPTES
sp.p: All as yet. It may be that either the enchantress shall die or else be discovered. If either happen I will then practise the utmost of my art. In the mean season, about this grove would I have a watch, and the first living thing that toucheth Endymion to be taken.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Corsites, what say you, will you undertake this?

sp.speaker: CORSITES
sp.p: Good madam, pardon me; I was overtaken too late. I should rather break into the midst of a main battle than again fall into the hands of those fair babies.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Well, I will provide others. Pythagoras and Gyptes, you shall yet remain in my court till I hear what may be done in this matter.

sp.speaker: PYTHAGORAS
sp.p: We attend.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Let us go in.

div2.stage: Exeunt. [Endymion continues asleep on his lunary bed, near a tree, but perhaps curtained off during the entr'acte music.]

div2.head: Actus Quintus, Scaena Prima

sp.speaker: SAMIAS
sp.p: Eumenides hath told such strange tales as I may well wonder at them but never believe them.

sp.speaker: DARES
sp.p: The other old man, what a sad speech used he, that caused us almost all to weep! Cynthia is so desirous to know the experiment of her own virtue, and so willing to ease Endymion's hard fortune, that she no sooner heard the discourse but she made herself in a readiness to try the event.

sp.speaker: SAMIAS
sp.p: We will also see the event. But whist! Here cometh Cynthia with all her train. Let us sneak in amongst them.

div2.stage: Enter Cynthia, Floscula, Semele, Panelion etc
[Eumenides, Zontes, Gyptes, and Pythagoras. Samias and Dares join the throng.]

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Eumenides, it cannot sink into my head that I should be signified by that sacred fountain, for many things are there in the world to which those words may be applied.

sp.speaker: EUMENIDES
sp.p: Good madam, vouchsafe but to try, else shall I think myself most unhappy that I asked not my sweet mistress.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Will you not yet tell me her name?

sp.speaker: EUMENIDES
sp.p: Pardon me, good madam, for if Endymion awake he shall. Myself have sworn never to reveal it.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Well, let us to Endymion. [They approach the sleeping Endymion.] I will not be so stately, good Endymion, not to stoop to do thee good; and if thy liberty consist in a kiss from me, thou shalt have it. And although my mouth hath been heretofore as untouched as my thoughts, yet now to recover thy life (though to restore thy youth it be impossible) I will do that to Endymion which yet never mortal man could boast of heretofore, nor shall ever hope for hereafter.

sp.speaker: EUMENIDES
sp.p: Madam, he beginneth to stir.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Soft, Eumenides. Stand still.

sp.speaker: EUMENIDES
sp.p: Ah, I see his eyes almost open.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: I command thee once again, stir not. I will stand behind him.

div2.stage: [She stands where Endymion will not see her at first.]

sp.speaker: PANELION
sp.p: What do I see, Endymion almost awake?

sp.speaker: EUMENIDES
sp.p: Endymion, Endymion, art thou deaf or dumb? Or hath this long sleep taken away thy memory? Ah, my sweet Endymion, seest thou not Eumenides, thy faithful friend, thy faithful Eumenides, who for thy safety hath been careless of his own content? Speak, Endymion, Endymion, Endymion!

sp.speaker: ENDYMION
sp.p: Endymion? I call to mind such a name.

sp.speaker: EUMENIDES
sp.p: Hast thou forgotten thyself, Endymion? Then do I not marvel thou rememberest not thy friend. I tell thee thou art Endymion and I Eumenides. Behold also Cynthia, by whose favour thou art awaked, and by whose virtue thou shalt continue thy natural course.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Endymion, speak, sweet Endymion. Knowest thou not Cynthia?

sp.speaker: ENDYMION
sp.p: O heavens, whom do I behold? Fair Cynthia, divine Cynthia?

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: I am Cynthia, and thou Endymion.

sp.speaker: ENDYMION
sp.p: Endymion? What do I hear? What, a grey beard? Hollow eyes? Withered body? Decayed limbs? And all in one night?

sp.speaker: EUMENIDES
sp.p: One night? Thou hast here slept forty years, by what enchantress as yet it is not known. And behold, the twig to which thou laidst thy head is now become a tree. Callest thou not Eumenides to remembrance?

sp.speaker: ENDYMION
sp.p: Thy name I do remember by the sound, but thy favour I do not yet call to mind. Only divine Cynthia, to whom time, fortune, destiny, and death are subject, I see and remember, and in all humility I regard and reverence.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: You have good cause to remember Eumenides, who hath for thy safety forsaken his own solace.

sp.speaker: ENDYMION
sp.p: Am I that Endymion who was wont in court to lead my life, and in jousts, tourneys, and arms to exercise my youth? Am I that Endymion?

sp.speaker: EUMENIDES
sp.p: Thou art that Endymion and I Eumenides. Wilt thou not yet call me to remembrance?

sp.speaker: ENDYMION
sp.p: Ah, sweet Eumenides, I now perceive thou art he, and that myself have the name of Endymion. But that this should be my body I doubt; for how could my curled locks be turned to grey hairs and my strong body to a dying weakness, having waxed old and not knowing it?

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Well, Endymion, arise. A while sit down, for that thy limbs are stiff and not able to stay thee, and tell what hast thou seen in thy sleep all this while? What dreams, visions, thoughts, and fortunes? For it is impossible but in so long time thou shouldst see things strange.

sp.speaker: ENDYMION
sp.p: Fair Cynthia, I will rehearse what I have seen, humbly desiring that when I exceed in length, you give me warning, that I may end. For to utter all I have to speak would be troublesome, although haply the strangeness may somewhat abate the tediousness.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Well, Endymion, begin.

sp.speaker: ENDYMION
sp.p: Methought I saw a lady passing fair but very mischievous, who in the one hand carried a knife with which she offered to cut my throat, and in the other a looking glass, wherein, seeing how ill anger became ladies, she refrained from intended violence. She was accompanied with other damsels, one of which, with a stern countenance, and as it were with a settled malice engraven in her eyes, provoked her to execute mischief. Another with visage sad, and constant only in sorrow, with her arms crossed, and watery eyes, seemed to lament my fortune, but durst not offer to prevent the force. I started in my sleep, feeling my very veins to swell and my sinews to stretch with fear, and such a cold sweat bedewed all my body that death itself could not be so terrible as the vision.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: A strange sight. Gyptes at our better leisure shall expound it.

sp.speaker: ENDYMION
sp.p: After long debating with herself, mercy overcame anger, and there appeared in her heavenly face such a divine majesty, mingled with a sweet mildness, that I was ravished with the sight above measure, and wished that I might have enjoyed the sight without end. And so she departed with the other ladies, of which the one retained still an unmovable cruelty, the other a constant pity.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Poor Endymion, how wast thou affrighted! What else?

sp.speaker: ENDYMION
sp.p: After her immediately appeared an aged man with a beard as white as snow, carrying in his hand a book with three leaves, and speaking, as I remember, these words: 'Endymion, receive this book with three leaves, in which are contained counsels, policies, and pictures.' And with that, he offered me the book, which I rejected; wherewith moved with a disdainful pity, he rent the first leaf in a thousand shivers. The second time he offered it, which I refused also; at which, bending his brows and pitching his eyes fast to the ground as though they were fixed to the earth and not again to be removed, then suddenly casting them up to the heavens, he tore in a rage the second leaf and offered the book only with one leaf. I know not whether fear to offend or desire to know some strange thing moved me; I took the book, and so the old man vanished.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: What didst thou imagine was in the last leaf?

sp.speaker: ENDYMION
sp.p: There –ay, portrayed to life– with a cold quaking in every joint, I beheld many wolves barking at thee, Cynthia, who, having ground their teeth to bite, did with striving bleed themselves to death. There might I see Ingratitude with an hundred eyes, gazing for benefits, and with a thousand teeth gnawing on the bowels wherein she was bred. Treachery stood all clothed in white, with a smiling countenance but both her hands bathed in blood. Envy, with a pale and meagre face, whose body was so lean that one might tell all her bones, and whose garment was so tattered that it was easy to number every thread, stood shooting at stars, whose darts fell down again on her own face. There might I behold drones, or beetles, I know not how to term them, creeping under the wings of a princely eagle, who, being carried into her nest, sought there to suck that vein that would have killed the eagle. I mused that things so base should attempt a fact so barbarous or durst imagine a thing so bloody. And many other things, madam, the repetition whereof may at your better leisure seem more pleasing; for bees surfeit sometimes with honey, and the gods are glutted with harmony, and Your Highness may be dulled with delight.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: I am content to be dieted; therefore let us in. Eumenides, see that Endymion be well tended, lest, either eating immoderately or sleeping again too long, he fall into a deadly surfeit or into his former sleep. See this also be proclaimed: that whosoever will discover this practice shall have of Cynthia infinite thanks and no small rewards.

div2.stage: Exit, [attended by her courtly entourage. Floscula, Endymion, and Eumenides remain.]

sp.speaker: FLOSCULA
sp.p: Ah, Endymion, none so joyful as Floscula of thy restoring!

sp.speaker: EUMENIDES
sp.p: Yes, Floscula, let Eumenides be somewhat gladder, and do not that wrong to the settled friendship of a man as to compare it with the light affection of a woman. –Ah, my dear friend Endymion, suffer me to die with gazing at thee!

sp.speaker: ENDYMION
sp.p: Eumenides, thy friendship is immortal and not to be conceived, and thy good will, Floscula, better than I have deserved. But let us all wait on Cynthia. I marvel Semele speaketh not a word.

sp.speaker: EUMENIDES
sp.p: Because if she do she loseth her tongue.

sp.speaker: ENDYMION
sp.p: But how prospereth your love?

sp.speaker: EUMENIDES
sp.p: I never yet spake word since your sleep.

sp.speaker: ENDYMION
sp.p: I doubt not but your affection is old and your appetite cold.

sp.speaker: EUMENIDES
sp.p: No, Endymion, thine hath made it stronger, and now are my sparks grown to flames and my fancies almost to frenzies. But let us follow, and within we will debate all this matter at large.

sp.speaker: TOPHAS
sp.p: Epi, love hath jostled my liberty from the wall and taken the upper hand of my reason.

sp.speaker: EPITON
sp.p: Let me then trip up the heels of your affection and thrust your good will into the gutter.

sp.speaker: TOPHAS
sp.p: No, Epi, love is a lord of misrule, and keepeth Christmas in my corpse.

sp.speaker: EPITON
sp.p: No doubt there is good cheer. What dishes of delight doth his lordship feast you withal?

sp.speaker: TOPHAS
sp.p: First, with a great platter of plum-porridge of pleasure, wherein is stewed the mutton of mistrust.

sp.speaker: EPITON
sp.p: Excellent love-lap!

sp.speaker: TOPHAS
sp.p: Then cometh a pie of patience, a hen of honey, a goose of gall, a capon of care, and many other viands, some sweet and some sour, which proveth love to be as it was said of in old years: dulce venenum .

sp.speaker: EPITON
sp.p: A brave banquet!

sp.speaker: TOPHAS
sp.p: But Epi, I pray thee feel on my chin; something pricketh me. What dost thou feel or see?

sp.speaker: EPITON
sp.p: [Examining his chin] There are three or four little hairs.

sp.speaker: TOPHAS
sp.p: I pray thee call it my beard. How shall I be troubled when this young spring shall grow to a great wood!

sp.speaker: EPITON
sp.p: O, sir, your chin is but a quiller yet. You will be most majestical when it is full fledge. But I marvel that you love Dipsas, that old crone.

sp.speaker: TOPHAS
sp.p: Agnosco veteris vestigia flamma , I love the smoke of an old fire.

sp.speaker: EPITON
sp.p: Why, she is so cold that no fire can thaw her thoughts.

sp.speaker: TOPHAS
sp.p: It is an old goose, Epi, that will eat no oats; old kine will kick, old rats gnaw cheese, and old sacks will have much patching. I prefer an old cony before a rabbit-sucker, and an ancient hen before a young chicken peeper.

p.seg: My master loveth antique work.

sp.speaker: TOPHAS
sp.p: Give me a pippin that is withered like an old wife.

sp.speaker: EPITON
sp.p: Good, sir.

sp.speaker: TOPHAS
sp.p: Then a contrario sequitur argumentum. Give me a wife that looks like an old pippin.

p.seg: Nothing hath made my master a fool but flat scholarship.

sp.speaker: TOPHAS
sp.p: Knowest thou not that old wine is best?

sp.speaker: EPITON
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: TOPHAS
sp.p: And thou knowest that like will to like?

sp.speaker: EPITON
sp.p: Ay.

sp.speaker: TOPHAS
sp.p: And thou knowest that Venus loved the best wine?

sp.speaker: EPITON
sp.p: So.

sp.speaker: TOPHAS
sp.p: Then I conclude that Venus was an old woman in an old cup of wine. For, est Venus in vinis, ignis in igne fruit.

sp.speaker: EPITON
sp.p: O lepidum caput , O madcap master! You were worthy to win Dipsas, where she as old again, for in your love you have worn the nap of your wit quite off and made it threadbare. But soft, who comes here?

sp.speaker: TOPHAS
sp.p: My solicitors.

sp.speaker: SAMIAS
sp.p: All hail, Sir Tophas! How feel you yourself?

sp.speaker: TOPHAS
sp.p: Stately in every joint, which the common people term stiffness. Doth Dipsas stoop? Will she yield? Will she bend?

sp.speaker: DARES
sp.p: O, sir, as much as you would wish, for her chin almost toucheth her knees.

sp.speaker: EPITON
sp.p: Master, she is bent, I warrant you.

sp.speaker: TOPHAS
sp.p: What conditions doth she ask?

sp.speaker: SAMIAS
sp.p: She hath vowed she will never love any that hath not a tooth in his head less than she.

sp.speaker: TOPHAS
sp.p: How many hath she?

sp.speaker: DARES
sp.p: One.

sp.speaker: EPITON
sp.p: That goeth hard, master, for then you must have none.

sp.speaker: TOPHAS
sp.p: A small request, and agreeable to the gravity of her years. What should a wise man do with his mouth full of bones like a charnel house? The turtle true hath ne'er a tooth.

p.seg: Thy master is in a notable vein, that will lose his teeth to be like a turtle.
Let him lose his tongue too, I care not.

sp.speaker: DARES
sp.p: Nay, you must also have no nails, for she long since hath cast hers.

sp.speaker: TOPHAS
sp.p: That I yield to. What a quiet life shall Dipsas and I lead, when we can neither bite nor scratch! You may see, youths, how age provides for peace.

p.seg: How shall we do to make him leave his love? For we never spake to her.
Let me alone.

sp.speaker: TOPHAS
sp.p: I honour her for her cunning, for now, when I am weary of walking on two legs, what a pleasure may she do me to turn me to some goodly ass and help me to four!

sp.speaker: DARES
sp.p: Nay then, I must tell you the truth: her husband Geron is come home, who this fifty years hath had her to wife.

sp.speaker: TOPHAS
sp.p: What do I hear? Hath she an husband? Go to the sexton and tell him Desire is dead, and will him to dig his grave. Oh heavens, an husband? What death is agreeable to my fortune?

sp.speaker: SAMIAS
sp.p: Be not desperate, and we will help you to find a young lady.

sp.speaker: TOPHAS
sp.p: I love no Grissels; they are so brittle they will crack like glass, or so dainty that if they be touched they are straight of the fashion of wax. Animus maioribus instat ; I desire old matrons. What a sight would it be to embrace one whose hair were as orient as the pearl, whose teeth shall be so pure a watchet that they shall stain the truest turquoise, whose nose shall throw more beams from it than the fiery carbuncle, whose eyes shall be environed about with redness exceeding the deepest coral, and whose lips might compare with silver for the paleness! Such a one if you can help me to, I will by piecemeal curtail my affections toward Dipsas and walk my swelling thoughts till they be cold.

sp.speaker: EPITON
sp.p: Wisely provided. How say you, my friends, will you angle for my master's cause?

sp.speaker: SAMIAS
sp.p: Most willingly.

sp.speaker: DARES
sp.p: If we speed him not shortly, I will burn my cap. We will serve him of the spades, and dig and old wife out of the grave that shall be answerable to his gravity.

sp.speaker: TOPHAS
sp.p: Youths, adieu. He that bringeth me first news shall possess mine inheritance.

sp.speaker: DARES
sp.p: [To Epiton] What, is thy master landed?

sp.speaker: EPITON
sp.p: Know you not that my master is liber tenens ?

sp.speaker: SAMIAS
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: EPITON
sp.p: A freeholder. But I will after him.

sp.speaker: SAMIAS
sp.p: And we to hear what news of Endymion for the conclusion.

sp.speaker: PANELION
sp.p: Who would have thought that Tellus, being so fair by nature, so honourable by birth, so wise by education, would have entered into a mischief to the gods so odious, to men so detestable, and to her friend so malicious?

sp.speaker: ZONTES
sp.p: If Bagoa had not bewrayed it, how then should it have come to light? But we see that gold and fair words are of force to corrupt the strongest men, and therefore able to work silly women like wax.

sp.speaker: PANELION
sp.p: I marvel what Cynthia will determine in this cause.

sp.speaker: ZONTES
sp.p: I fear as in all causes: hear of it in justice and then judge of it in mercy. For how can it be that she that is unwilling to punish her deadliest foes with disgrace will revenge injuries of her train with death?

sp.speaker: PANELION
sp.p: That old witch Dipsas, in a rage, having understood her practice to be discovered, turned poor Bagoa to an aspen tree. But let us make haste and bring Tellus before Cynthia, for she was coming out after us.

sp.speaker: ZONTES
sp.p: Let us go.

div2.head: [SCENE 4]
div2.stage: Eumenides[, Geron, Pythagoras, Gyptes, and Sir Tophas.
A tree stands by the lunary bank, as in IV.iii and V.i].

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Dipsas, thy years are not so many as thy vices, yet more in number than commonly nature doth afford or justice should permit. Hast thou almost these fifty years practised that detested wickedness of witchcraft? Wast thou so simple as for to know the nature of simples, of all creatures to be most sinful? Thou hast threatened to turn my course awry and alter by thy damnable art the government that I now possess by the eternal gods. But know thou, Dipsas, and let all the enchanters know, that Cynthia, being placed for light on earth, is also protected by the powers of heaven. Breathe out thou mayst words, gather thou mayst herbs, find out thou mayst stones agreeable to thine art, yet of no force to appal my heart, in which courage is so rooted, and constant persuasion of the mercy of the gods so grounded, that all thy witchcraft I esteem as weak as the world doth thy case wretched. This noble gentleman Geron, once thy husband but now thy mortal hate, didst thou procure to live in a desert, almost desperate. Endymion, the flower of my court and the hope of succeeding time, hast thou bewitched by art before thou wouldst suffer him to flourish by nature.

sp.speaker: DIPSAS
sp.p: Madam, things past may be repented, not recalled. There is nothing so wicked that I have not done, nor anything so wished for as death. Yet among all the things that I committed, there is nothing so much tormenteth my rented and ransacked thoughts as that in the prime of my husband's youth I divorced him by my devilish art, for which, if to die might be amends, I would not live till tomorrow. If to live and still be more miserable would better content him, I would wish of all creatures to be oldest and ugliest.

sp.speaker: GERON
sp.p: Dipsas, thou hast made this difference between me and Endymion, that, being both young, thou hast caused me to wake in melancholy, losing the joys of my youth, and him to sleep, not remembering youth.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Stay, here cometh Tellus. We shall now know all.

sp.speaker: CORSITES
sp.p: [To Tellus] I would to Cynthia thou couldst make as good an excuse in truth as to me thou hast done by wit.

sp.speaker: TELLUS
sp.p: Truth shall be mine answer, and therefore I will not study for an excuse.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Is it possible, Tellus, that so few years should harbour so many mischiefs? Thy swelling pride have I borne because it is a thing that beauty maketh blameless, which, the more it exceedeth fairness in measure, the more it stretcheth itself in disdain. Thy devices against Corsites I smile at, for that wits the sharper they are, the shrewder they are. But this unacquainted and most unnatural practice with a vile enchantress against so noble a gentleman as Endymion I abhor as a thing most malicious, and will revenge as a deed most monstrous. And as for you, Dipsas, I will send you into the desert amongst wild beasts, and try whether you can cast lions, tigers, boars, and bears into as dead a sleep as you did Endymion, or turn them to trees as you have done Bagoa. But tell me, Tellus, what was the cause of this cruel part, far unfitting thy sex, in which nothing should be but simpleness, and much disagreeing from thy face, in which nothing seemed to be but softness?

sp.speaker: TELLUS
sp.p: Divine Cynthia, by whom I receive my life and am content to end it, I can neither excuse my fault without lying nor confess it without shame. Yet were it possible that in so heavenly thoughts as yours there could fall such earthly motions as mine, I would then hope, if not to be pardoned without extreme punishment, yet to be heard without great marvel.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Say on, Tellus. I cannot imagine anything that can colour such a cruelty.

sp.speaker: TELLUS
sp.p: Endymion, that Endymion, in the prime of his youth so ravished my heart with love that to obtain my desires I could not find means, nor to resist them reason. What was she that favoured not Endymion, being young, wise, honourable, and virtuous? Besides, what metal was she made of, be she mortal, that is not affected with the spice, nay infected with the poison, of that not-to-be-expressed yet always-to-be-felt love, which breaketh the brains and never bruiseth the brow, consumeth the heart and never toucheth the skin, and maketh a deep wound to be felt before any scar at all be seen? My heart, too tender to withstand such a divine fury, yielded to love –madam, I not without blushing confess, yielded to love.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: A strange effect of love, to work such an extreme hate. How say you, Endymion, all this was for love?

sp.speaker: ENDYMION
sp.p: I say, madam, then the gods send me a woman's hate.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: That were as bad, for then by contrary you should never sleep. But on, Tellus, let us hear the end.

sp.speaker: TELLUS
sp.p: Feeling a continual burning in all my bowels and a bursting almost in every vein, I could not smother the inward fire, but it must needs be perceived by the outward smoke; and, by the flying abroad of divers sparks, divers judged of my scalding flames. Endymion, as full of art as wit, marking mine eyes (in which he might see almost his own), my sighs (by which he might ever hear his name sounded), aimed at my heart (in which he was assured his person was imprinted), and by questions wrung out that which was ready to burst out. When he saw the depth of my affections, he swore that mine in respect of his were as fumes to Etna, valleys to Alps, ants to eagles, and nothing could be compared to my beauty but his love and eternity. Thus drawing a smooth shoe upon a crooked foot, he made me believe that (which all of our sex willingly acknowledge) I was beautiful, and to wonder (which indeed is a thing miraculous) that any of his sex should be faithful.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Endymion, how will you clear yourself?

sp.speaker: ENDYMION
sp.p: Madam, by mine own accuser.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Well, Tellus, proceed, but briefly, lest, taking delight in uttering thy love, thou offend us with the length of it.

sp.speaker: TELLUS
sp.p: I will, madam, quickly make an end of my love and my tale. Finding continual increase of my tormenting thoughts, and that the enjoying of my love made deeper wounds than the entering into it, I could find no means to ease my grief but to follow Endymion, and continually to have him in the object of mine eyes, who had me slave and subject to his love. But in the moment that I feared his falsehood, and fried myself most in mine affections, I found (ah, grief! even then I lost myself), I found him in most melancholy and desperate terms, cursing his stars, his state, the earth, the heavens, the world, an all for the love of–

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Of whom? Tellus, speak boldly.

sp.speaker: TELLUS
sp.p: Madam, I dare not utter for fear to offend.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Speak, I say. Who dare take offence if thou be commanded by Cynthia?

sp.speaker: TELLUS
sp.p: For the love of Cynthia.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: For my love, Tellus? That were strange. Endymion, is it true?

sp.speaker: ENDYMION
sp.p: In all things, madam. Tellus doth not speak false.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: What will this breed to in the end? Well, Endymion, we shall hear all.

sp.speaker: TELLUS
sp.p: I, seeing my hopes turned to mishaps, and a settled dissembling towards me, and an unmovable desire to Cynthia, forgetting both myself and my sex, fell unto this unnatural hate. For knowing your virtues, Cynthia, to be immortal, I could not have an imagination to withdraw him; and finding mine own affections unquenchable, I could not carry the mind that any else should possess what I had pursued. For though in majesty, beauty, virtue, and dignity I always humbled and yielded myself to Cynthia, yet in affections I esteemed myself equal with the goddesses, and all other creatures, according to their states, with myself. For stars to their bigness have their lights, and the sun hath no more. And little pitchers, when they can hold no more, are as full as great vessels that run over. Thus, madam, in all truth have I uttered the unhappiness of my love and the cause of my hate, yielding wholly to that divine judgement which never erred for want of wisdom or envied for too much partiality.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: How say you, my lords, to this matter? But what say you, Endymion, hath Tellus told truth?

sp.speaker: ENDYMION
sp.p: Madam, in all things, but in that she said I loved her and swore to honour her.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Was there such a time whenas for my love thou didst vow thyself to death, and in respect of it loathed thy life? Speak, Endymion. I will not revenge it with hate.

sp.speaker: ENDYMION
sp.p: The time was, madam, and is, and ever shall be, that I honoured Your Highness above all the world; but to stretch it so far as to call it love, I never durst. There hath none pleased mine eye but Cynthia, none delighted mine ears but Cynthia, none possessed my heart but Cynthia. I have forsaken all other fortunes to follow Cynthia, and here I stand ready to die if it please Cynthia. Such a difference hath the gods set between our states that all must be duty, loyalty, and reverence; nothing, without it vouchsafe Your Highness, be termed love. My unspotted thoughts, my languishing body, my discontented life, let them obtain by princely favour that which to challenge they must not presume, only wishing of impossibilities; with imagination of which I will spend my spirits, and to myself, that no creature may hear, softly call it love. And if any urge to utter what I whisper, then will I name it honour. From this sweet contemplation if I be not driven, I shall live of all men the most content, taking more pleasure in mine aged thoughts than ever I did in my youthful actions.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Endymion, this honourable respect of thine shall be christened 'love' in thee, and my reward for it 'favour'. Persevere, Endymion, in loving me, and I account more strength in a true heart than in a walled city. I have laboured to win all, and study to keep such as I have won; but those that neither my favour can move to continue constant, nor my offered benefits get to be faithful, the gods shall either reduce to truth or revenge their treacheries with justice. Endymion, continue as thou hast begun, and thou shalt find that Cynthia shineth not on thee in vain.

div2.stage: [Endymion's youthful looks are restored to him.]

sp.speaker: ENDYMION
sp.p: Your highness hath blessed me, and your words have again restored my youth. Methinks I feel my joints strong, and these mouldy hairs to moult, and all by your virtue, Cynthia, into whose hands the balance that weigheth time and fortune are committed.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: What, young again? Then it is pity to punish Tellus.

sp.speaker: TELLUS
sp.p: Ah, Endymion, now I know thee and ask pardon of thee. Suffer me still to wish thee well.

sp.speaker: ENDYMION
sp.p: Tellus, Cynthia must command what she will.

sp.speaker: FLOSCULA
sp.p: Endymion, I rejoice to see thee in thy former estate.

sp.speaker: ENDYMION
sp.p: Good Floscula, to thee also am I in my former affections.

sp.speaker: EUMENIDES
sp.p: Endymion, the comfort of my life, how am I ravished with a joy matchless, saving only the enjoying of my mistress!

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Endymion, you must now tell who Eumenides shrineth for his saint.

sp.speaker: ENDYMION
sp.p: Semele, madam.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Semele, Eumenides? Is it Semele? The very wasp of all women, whose tongue stingeth as much as an adder's tooth?

sp.speaker: EUMENIDES
sp.p: It is Semele, Cynthia, the possessing of whose love must only prolong my life.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Nay, sith Endymion is restored, we will have all parties pleased. Semele, are you content after so long trial of his faith, such rare secrecy, such unspotted love, to take Eumenides? –Why speak you not? Not a word?

sp.speaker: ENDYMION
sp.p: Silence, madam, consents. That is most true.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: It is true, Endymion. Eumenides, take Semele. Take her, I say.

sp.speaker: EUMENIDES
sp.p: Humble thanks, madam. Now only do I begin to live.

sp.speaker: SEMELE
sp.p: A hard choice, madam, either to be married if I say nothing or to lose my tongue if I speak a word. Yet do I rather choose to have my tongue cut out than my heart distempered. I will not have him.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Speaks the parrot? She shall nod hereafter with signs. Cut off her tongue, nay, her head, that, having a servant of honourable birth, honest manners, and true love, will not be persuaded!

sp.speaker: SEMELE
sp.p: He is no faithful lover, madam, for then would he have asked his mistress.

sp.speaker: GERON
sp.p: Had he not been faithful, he had never seen into the fountain, and so lost his friend and mistress.

sp.speaker: EUMENIDES
sp.p: Thine own thoughts, sweet Semele, witness against thy words, for what hast thou found in my life but love? And as yet what have I found in my love but bitterness? Madam, pardon Semele, and let my tongue ransom hers.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Thy tongue, Eumenides? What shouldst thou live, wanting a tongue to blaze the beauty of Semele? Well, Semele, I will not command love, for it cannot be enforced. Let me entreat it.

sp.speaker: SEMELE
sp.p: I am content Your Highness shall command, for now only do I think Eumenides faithful, that is willing to lose his tongue for my sake; yet loath, because it should do me better service. Madam, I accept of Eumenides.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: I thank you, Semele.

sp.speaker: EUMENIDES
sp.p: Ah, happy Eumenides, that hast a friend so faithful and a mistress so fair! With what sudden mischief will the gods daunt this excess of joy? Sweet Semele, I live or die as thou wilt.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: What shall become of Tellus? Tellus, you know Endymion is vowed to a service from which death cannot remove him. Corsites casteth still a lovely look towards you. How say you, will you have your Corsites and so receive pardon for all that is past?

sp.speaker: TELLUS
sp.p: Madam, most willingly.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: But I cannot tell whether Corsites be agreed.

sp.speaker: CORSITES
sp.p: Ay, madam, more happy to enjoy Tellus than the monarchy of the world.

sp.speaker: EUMENIDES
sp.p: Why, she caused you to be pinched with fairies.

sp.speaker: CORSITES
sp.p: Ay, but her fairness hath pinched my heart more deeply.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Well, enjoy thy love. But what have you wrought in the castle, Tellus?

sp.speaker: TELLUS
sp.p: Only the picture of Endymion.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Then so much of Endymion as his picture cometh to, possess and play withal.

sp.speaker: CORSITES
sp.p: Ah, my sweet Tellus, my love shall be as thy beauty is: matchless.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Now it resteth, Dipsas, that if thou wilt forswear that vile art of enchanting, Geron hath promised again to receive thee; otherwise, If thou be wedded to that wickedness, I must and will see it punished to the uttermost.

sp.speaker: DIPSAS
sp.p: Madam, I renounce both substance and shadow of that most horrible and hateful trade, vowing to the gods continual penance and to Your Highness obedience.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: How say you, Geron, will you admit her to your wife?

sp.speaker: GERON
sp.p: Ay, with more joy than I did the first day, for nothing could happen to make me happy but only her forsaking that lewd and detestable course. Dipsas, I embrace thee.

sp.speaker: DIPSAS
sp.p: And I thee, Geron, to whom I will hereafter recite the cause of these my first follies.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Well, Endymion, nothing resteth now but that we depart. Thou hast my favour, Tellus her friend, Eumenides in paradise with his Semele, Geron contented with Dipsas.

sp.speaker: TOPHAS
sp.p: Nay, soft. I cannot handsomely go to bed without Bagoa.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Well, Sir Tophas, it may be there are more virtues in me than myself knoweth of, for Endymion I awaked, and at my words he waxed young. I will try whether I can turn this tree again to thy true love.

sp.speaker: TOPHAS
sp.p: Turn her to a true love or false, so she be a wench I care not.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Bagoa, Cynthia putteth an end to thy hard fortunes, for, being turned to a tree for revealing a truth, I will recover thee again if in my power be the effect of truth.

sp.speaker: TOPHAS
sp.p: Bagoa? A bots upon thee!

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Come my lords, let us in. You, Gyptes and Pythagoras, if you cannot content yourselves in our court to fall from vain follies of philosophers to such virtues as are here practised, you shall be entertained according to your deserts, for Cynthia is no stepmother to strangers.

sp.speaker: PYTHAGORAS
sp.p: I had rather in Cynthia's court spend ten years than in Greece one hour.

sp.speaker: GYPTES
sp.p: And I choose rather to live by the sight of Cynthia than by the possessing of all Egypt.

sp.speaker: CYNTHIA
sp.p: Then follow.

sp.speaker: EUMENIDES
sp.p: We all attend.

A man walking abroad, the wind and sun strove for sovereignty; the one with his blast, the other with his beams. The wind blew hard; the man wrapped his garment about him harder. It blustered more strongly; he then girt it fast to him. 'I cannot prevail', said the wind. The sun casting her crystal beams began to warm the man; he unloosed his gown. Yet it shined brighter; he then put it off. 'I yield', said the wind, 'for if thou continue shining he will also put off his coat'. Dread sovereign, the malicious that seek to overthrow us with threats do but stiffen our thoughts and make them sturdier in storms. But if Your Highness vouchsafe with your favourable beams to glance upon us, we shall not only stoop, but with all humility lay both our hands and hearts at Your Majesty’s feet.
